claim: Methionine restriction (MR) dramatically extends the healthspan of several organisms.
source: Methionine restriction (MR) dramatically extends the healthspan of several organisms.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Methionine-restricted rodents have less age-related pathology and increased longevity as compared with controls.
source: Methionine-restricted rodents have less age-related pathology and increased longevity as compared with controls
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies (Miller et al., 2005; Orentreich et al., 1993; Richie et al., 1994) mentioned in the Introduction.

claim: Recent studies suggest that humans might benefit similarly from methionine restriction.
source: recent studies suggest that humans might benefit similarly
evidence: Supported by citations (Dong et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2019; Johnson and Johnson, 2014) in the Introduction.

claim: The decreased IGF-1 signaling that results from MR likely underlies the benefits of this regimen.
source: Mechanistically, it is likely that the decreased IGF-1 signaling that results from MR underlies the benefits of this regimen.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Selenium supplementation inhibits IGF-1 signaling in rats.
source: Selenium supplementation inhibits IGF-1 signaling in rats
evidence: Supported by citation to Thorlacius-Ussing et al., 1987 in the Introduction.

claim: Feeding mice a diet supplemented with sodium selenite results in an MR-like phenotype, marked by protection against diet-induced obesity.
source: Indeed, we show that feeding mice a diet supplemented with sodium selenite results in an MR-like phenotype, marked by protection against diet-induced obesity
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Sodium selenite supplementation alters plasma levels of IGF-1, FGF-21, adiponectin, and leptin in mice.
source: feeding mice a diet supplemented with sodium selenite results in an MR-like phenotype, marked by protection against diet-induced obesity, as well as altered plasma levels of IGF-1, FGF-21, adiponectin, and leptin
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Selenomethionine supplementation results in a similar, albeit less robust response compared to sodium selenite.
source: Selenomethionine supplementation results in a similar, albeit less robust response
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Selenomethionine supplementation extends budding yeast lifespan.
source: Selenomethionine supplementation results in a similar, albeit less robust response, and also extends budding yeast lifespan.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A and 9B.

claim: Selenium supplementation is sufficient to produce MR-like healthspan benefits for yeast and mammals.
source: Our results indicate that selenium supplementation is sufficient to produce MR-like healthspan benefits for yeast and mammals.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Rats fed a methionine-restricted diet are substantially longer-lived than their control-fed counterparts.
source: For example, rats fed a methionine-restricted diet are substantially longer-lived than their control-fed counterparts and show a marked amelioration of age-related pathologies
evidence: Supported by citations (Miller et al., 2005; Orentreich et al., 1993; Richie et al., 1994).

claim: Methionine-restricted mice receive similar benefits to methionine-restricted rats.
source: rats fed a methionine-restricted diet are substantially longer-lived than their control-fed counterparts and show a marked amelioration of age-related pathologies; methionine-restricted mice receive similar benefits
evidence: Supported by citations (Miller et al., 2005; Orentreich et al., 1993; Richie et al., 1994).

claim: MR improves metabolic health in rodents, marked by reduced white adipose tissue accumulation, amelioration of liver steatosis, and improved glycemic control.
source: Among the varied benefits of MR to rodents, there is an improvement in metabolic health, marked by reduced white adipose tissue accumulation, amelioration of liver steatosis (aka, 'fatty liver disease'), and improved glycemic control (Malloy et al., 2006; Malloy et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations (Malloy et al., 2006; Malloy et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2005).

claim: MR provides complete protection against diet-induced obesity in rodents.
source: In fact, these metabolic benefits are so robust that MR provides complete protection against diet-induced obesity, which results from feeding animals a high-fat diet meant to approximate the human Western diet (Ables et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation (Ables et al., 2012).

claim: Methionine-restricted animals demonstrate altered plasma levels of IGF-1, FGF-21, adiponectin, and leptin.
source: In addition, as part of the multi-faceted response to MR, restricted animals also demonstrate altered plasma levels of the nutrient- and stress-sensing hormones IGF-1, FGF-21, adiponectin, and leptin.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations and data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The response to MR is conserved throughout phylogeny.
source: Recent studies have suggested that the response to MR is conserved throughout phylogeny
evidence: Supported by citations (Dong et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2019; Johnson and Johnson, 2014).

claim: The vegan diet is naturally low in proteins and free amino acids.
source: As the vegan diet is naturally low in proteins and free amino acids, a methionine-restricted diet is technically feasible for humans (McCarty et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation (McCarty et al., 2009).

claim: A methionine-restricted diet is technically feasible for humans.
source: As the vegan diet is naturally low in proteins and free amino acids, a methionine-restricted diet is technically feasible for humans (McCarty et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation (McCarty et al., 2009).

claim: A methionine-restricted diet might not be practical for all individuals.
source: However, such a diet might not be practical for all individuals, and as a result, widespread adherence is likely to be problematic.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about practical implementation.

claim: A decrease in circulating IGF-1 levels is likely responsible for many, if not all, of the health benefits of MR.
source: An important clue for the identification and development of an MR-like intervention that is effective in a methionine-replete context is the observation that a decrease in the circulating levels of the energy-regulating hormone IGF-1 (Ables et al., 2012; Malloy et al., 2006) is likely responsible for many, if not all, of the health benefits of MR.
evidence: Supported by citations (Ables et al., 2012; Malloy et al., 2006) and experimental evidence discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Feeding a methionine-restricted diet to long-lived dwarf mice with low IGF-1 levels failed to further extend the lifespan of these animals.
source: Specifically, in an exhaustive study comparing the effects of MR and impairment of growth hormone (GH)/IGF-1 signaling on healthspan, it was found that feeding a methionine-restricted diet to long-lived dwarf mice with low IGF-1 levels failed to further extend the lifespan of these animals (Brown-Borg et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation (Brown-Borg et al., 2014).

claim: The lack of additive or synergistic effects of MR and GH/IGF-1 impairment on longevity suggests that MR extends healthspan primarily by lowering IGF-1 levels.
source: Given that MR reduces circulating IGF-1 levels, the lack of either additive or synergistic effects of MR and GH/IGF-1 impairment on overall longevity suggests that MR extends healthspan primarily (and possibly even entirely) by lowering IGF-1 levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited study (Brown-Borg et al., 2014).

claim: GH injections abrogate the MR phenotype of methionine-restricted rats.
source: Indeed, unpublished studies from the Orentreich Foundation found that GH injections abrogate the MR phenotype of methionine-restricted rats (not shown).
evidence: This is stated as unpublished data from the authors' institution.

claim: Short-lived GH-overexpressing transgenic mice show an impaired response to MR.
source: In addition, Brown-Borg et al. recently demonstrated that short-lived GH-overexpressing transgenic mice show an impaired response to MR (Brown-Borg et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation (Brown-Borg et al., 2018).

claim: Many healthspan-extending dietary interventions feature impaired IGF-1 signaling, including calorie restriction, intermittent fasting, ketogenic diet, and protein restriction.
source: Indeed, in addition to MR, many other healthspan-extending dietary interventions are known to feature impaired IGF-1 signaling, including calorie restriction (CR), intermittent fasting, ketogenic diet, and protein restriction (Ables et al., 2012; Boden et al., 2005; Breese et al., 1991; Dunn et al., 1997; Fontana et al., 2008; Fraser et al., 2000; Malloy et al., 2006; Miller et al., 2005; Rahmani et al., 2019; Scarth, 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Ables et al., 2012; Boden et al., 2005; Breese et al., 1991; Dunn et al., 1997; Fontana et al., 2008; Fraser et al., 2000; Malloy et al., 2006; Miller et al., 2005; Rahmani et al., 2019; Scarth, 2006).

claim: Selenium supplementation limits the growth of young rats.
source: Prompted by the observation that selenium supplementation limits the growth of young rats, as well as the fact that selenium can accumulate in the pituitary, Thorlacius-Ussing et al. explored whether GH/IGF-1 signaling might be impaired by this intervention (Thorlacius-Ussing et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation (Thorlacius-Ussing et al., 1987).

claim: Selenium can accumulate in the pituitary.
source: Prompted by the observation that selenium supplementation limits the growth of young rats, as well as the fact that selenium can accumulate in the pituitary, Thorlacius-Ussing et al. explored whether GH/IGF-1 signaling might be impaired by this intervention (Thorlacius-Ussing et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation (Thorlacius-Ussing et al., 1987).

claim: Plasma levels of GH were reduced by 77% in rats exposed to sodium selenite as compared with control animals.
source: The authors found that plasma levels of GH were reduced by 77% in rats exposed to sodium selenite as compared with control animals.
evidence: Supported by citation (Thorlacius-Ussing et al., 1987).

claim: Circulating IGF-1 levels were reduced by 83% in selenium-supplemented rats.
source: Additionally, as would be expected given the fact that GH signaling controls the release of IGF-1 into the bloodstream, circulating IGF-1 levels were also reduced by 83% in selenium-supplemented animals.
evidence: Supported by citation (Thorlacius-Ussing et al., 1987).

claim: Sodium selenite supplementation completely protected male mice against the dramatic weight gain observed for control-fed animals.
source: Using this approach, we found that sodium selenite supplementation completely protected male mice against the dramatic weight gain observed for control-fed animals (Figure 1A,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1D.

claim: The protection against diet-induced obesity conferred by sodium selenite supplementation was essentially identical to that observed for methionine-restricted male mice.
source: In fact, the protection against diet-induced obesity conferred by sodium selenite supplementation was essentially identical to that observed for methionine-restricted male mice (Figure 1A,D,G,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, 1D, 1G, and 1H.

claim: Both MR and sodium selenite supplementation resulted in a robust reduction in the accumulation of inguinal adipose tissue (MR, 82%; CF-SS, 83%) in male mice.
source: In particular, both interventions resulted in a robust reduction in the accumulation of inguinal (MR, 82%; CF-SS, 83%) as well as perigonadal (MR, 78%; CF-SS, 80%) adipose tissue (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and 1H.

claim: Both MR and sodium selenite supplementation resulted in a robust reduction in the accumulation of perigonadal adipose tissue (MR, 78%; CF-SS, 80%) in male mice.
source: In particular, both interventions resulted in a robust reduction in the accumulation of inguinal (MR, 82%; CF-SS, 83%) as well as perigonadal (MR, 78%; CF-SS, 80%) adipose tissue (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and 1H.

claim: At 16 weeks, the average total body mass of sodium selenite-supplemented male animals was slightly higher than that of methionine-restricted animals (25.6 g vs 21.0 g).
source: At the end of the experiment (16 weeks), the average total body mass of sodium selenite-supplemented animals was slightly higher than that of methionine-restricted animals (25.6 g vs 21.0 g; Figure 1A,D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1D.

claim: The growth inhibitory effect associated with MR was somewhat less pronounced for sodium selenite supplementation in male mice.
source: Put another way, the growth inhibitory effect known to be associated with MR (Ables et al., 2012; Miller et al., 2005; Orentreich et al., 1993) was somewhat less pronounced for sodium selenite supplementation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the body mass data and supported by citations (Ables et al., 2012; Miller et al., 2005; Orentreich et al., 1993).

claim: Sodium selenite-supplemented male mice were protected against liver steatosis.
source: In addition, the smaller liver weights resulting from these two interventions were also nearly identical (0.63 g vs 0.68 g; Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that sodium selenite-supplemented male mice were, like their methionine-restricted littermates, protected against liver steatosis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Sodium selenite-containing food was consumed equivalently to the control diet by male mice.
source: With respect to absolute food consumption, sodium selenite-containing food was consumed equivalently to the control diet (Figure 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Male mice found sodium selenite-containing food to be just as palatable as the control diet and were not calorie-restricted.
source: Thus, male mice found sodium selenite-containing food to be just as palatable as the control diet and were not calorie-restricted.
evidence: This is an inference based on food consumption data shown in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: The total protection against diet-induced obesity enjoyed by male mice was directly due to sodium selenite supplementation.
source: This confirms that the total protection against diet-induced obesity enjoyed by male mice was directly due to sodium selenite supplementation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the food consumption and body mass data.

claim: MR ameliorated the diet-induced obesity of 9-month-old female mice.
source: Using 9-month-old female mice for these studies, we found that females of this age dramatically increased in weight (Figure 2A,D) and readily accumulated adipose tissue (Figure 2G,H) when fed a high-fat diet. In contrast, MR ameliorated the diet-induced obesity of female mice (Figure 2A,D,G,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, 2D, 2G, and 2H.

claim: This is the first time that MR has been reported to ameliorate diet-induced obesity in wild-type female mice.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first time that this has been reported for wild-type females.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: Sodium selenite supplementation protected female mice against diet-induced obesity more effectively than MR.
source: In any case, we were surprised to observe that not only does sodium selenite supplementation protect female mice against diet-induced obesity, it did so arguably more effectively than MR.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Sodium selenite-supplemented female mice demonstrated more robust decreases in both inguinal adiposity (81% less than controls) and perigonadal adiposity (80% less than controls) than did methionine-restricted littermates (53% and 56% less than controls).
source: Furthermore, sodium selenite-supplemented animals demonstrated more robust decreases in both inguinal adiposity (81% less than controls) and perigonadal adiposity (80% less than controls) than did methionine-restricted littermates (53% and 56% less than controls, inguinal and perigonadal; Figure 2G,H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G, 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The smaller body size and lower adiposity of sodium selenite-supplemented female mice were not due to reduced calorie intake.
source: Finally, and similar to the case for males, the smaller body size and lower adiposity of sodium selenite-supplemented female mice were not due to reduced calorie intake, as their food consumption was at least equivalent to control-fed animals, whether normalized for body weight or not (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Sodium selenite supplementation is sufficient to completely protect both male and female mice against diet-induced obesity.
source: In total, these experiments clearly demonstrate that sodium selenite supplementation is sufficient to completely protect both male and female mice against diet-induced obesity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Plasma IGF-1 levels were dramatically reduced in male mice by both MR and sodium selenite supplementation.
source: Indeed, we found plasma IGF-1 levels to be dramatically reduced in male mice by both MR and sodium selenite supplementation (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At 16 weeks, IGF-1 levels in male mice were reduced by 53% (MR) and 37% (CF-SS) as compared with control values.
source: At the conclusion of the experiment, IGF-1 levels were reduced by 53% (MR) and 37% (CF-SS), respectively, as compared with control values
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Male mice that had been fed methionine-restricted and sodium selenite-supplemented diets for 16 weeks showed reductions in circulating leptin of 98% and 96%, respectively, as compared with controls.
source: As an example, male mice that had been fed methionine-restricted and sodium selenite-supplemented diets for 16 weeks showed reductions in circulating leptin of 98% and 96%, respectively, as compared with controls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At all time-points assessed, the levels of adiponectin and FGF-21 in the plasma of sodium selenite-supplemented male mice did not show the increases typically observed for MR.
source: In other words, at all time-points assessed, the levels of adiponectin and FGF-21 in the plasma of sodium selenite-supplemented male mice did not show the increases typically observed for MR (Figure 3C,D) and were not significantly different from those of control animals.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Glucose and insulin were significantly reduced by MR and sodium selenite supplementation in male mice.
source: The final circulating analytes assessed for male mice were glucose and insulin, both of which were significantly reduced by MR and sodium selenite supplementation (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: The beneficial metabolic milieu conferred to male mice by selenium supplementation includes improved glycemic control.
source: This finding suggests that the beneficial metabolic milieu conferred to male mice by selenium supplementation also includes improved glycemic control
evidence: This is an inference based on the glucose and insulin data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: Selenium can regulate glucose metabolism and may be an 'insulin mimetic'.
source: and is consistent with a previous report that selenium can regulate glucose metabolism and may be an 'insulin mimetic' (Stapleton, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation (Stapleton, 2000).

claim: IGF-1 levels in female mice were decreased by sodium selenite supplementation as compared with control animals and were lower even than those resulting from MR.
source: For example, IGF-1 levels were decreased by sodium selenite supplementation as compared with control animals and were lower even than those resulting from MR (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At 8 weeks, the concentration of IGF-1 in female mice was decreased by 65% as compared with controls.
source: The most robust effect was observed at 8 weeks, when the concentration of IGF-1 was decreased by 65% as compared with controls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: At 16 weeks, leptin levels in female mice were 87% (CF-SS) and 63% (MR) lower than control levels.
source: At the terminal time-point, leptin levels were 87% (CF-SS) and 63% (MR) lower than control levels.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: After consuming the diets for 8 weeks, female animals demonstrated 34% (CF-SS) and 30% (MR) higher levels of adiponectin than control mice.
source: After consuming the diets for 8 weeks, animals demonstrated 34% (CF-SS) and 30% (MR) higher levels of adiponectin than control mice, as well as 40-fold (CF-SS) and 17-fold (MR) higher levels of FGF-21.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: After consuming the diets for 8 weeks, female animals demonstrated 40-fold (CF-SS) and 17-fold (MR) higher levels of FGF-21 than control mice.
source: After consuming the diets for 8 weeks, animals demonstrated 34% (CF-SS) and 30% (MR) higher levels of adiponectin than control mice, as well as 40-fold (CF-SS) and 17-fold (MR) higher levels of FGF-21.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Sodium selenite-supplemented females showed improved glycemic control, as both plasma glucose and plasma insulin levels were significantly reduced by this intervention at the 8-week and 16-week time-points.
source: In addition, sodium selenite-supplemented females also showed improved glycemic control, as both plasma glucose and plasma insulin levels were significantly reduced by this intervention at the 8-week and 16-week time-points (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claim: By all tested metrics, sodium selenite was found to recapitulate phenotypes associated with MR when fed to female mice.
source: Thus, by all tested metrics, sodium selenite was found to recapitulate phenotypes associated with MR when fed to female mice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The regulation of FGF-21 by sodium selenite supplementation is age-dependent.
source: Therefore, it is both notable and apparent that the regulation of FGF-21 by sodium selenite supplementation is age-dependent.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data comparing young (2-month-old) and older (8-month-old) male mice shown in Figure 3D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Selenium supplementation-dependent alterations in the plasma levels of adiponectin are sex-specific.
source: In contrast, adiponectin levels in male mice remained unaffected by this intervention, even in 8-month-old animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E). Thus, the latter finding suggests that selenium supplementation-dependent alterations in the plasma levels of adiponectin are sex-specific.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data comparing male and female mice shown in Figure 3C, Figure 4C, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Sodium selenite supplementation produces most, if not all, of several MR-associated beneficial physiological changes in both male and female mice.
source: In any case, taken together, our results indicate that sodium selenite supplementation produces most, if not all, of several MR-associated beneficial physiological changes in both male and female mice.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all experimental data presented in Figures 1-4.

claim: Sodium selenite supplementation did not produce a significant difference in plasma GH levels as compared with control-fed littermates in young male mice.
source: Although the values for GH levels (as well as their distributions) were as expected (Figure 5A), we did not detect a significant difference between samples from sodium selenite-supplemented animals and control-fed littermates.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: After GHRP-2 injection, circulating GH levels were approximately two orders of magnitude greater than those of mice not receiving GHRP-2 injections.
source: Using this approach, we found that circulating GH levels were approximately two orders of magnitude greater than those of mice not receiving GHRP-2 injections (Figure 5A,B), demonstrating the efficacy of this compound.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: No significant difference was detected between the levels of GH in sodium selenite-supplemented animals as compared with controls after GHRP-2 injection.
source: Despite this, we remained unable to detect a significant difference between the levels of GH in sodium selenite-supplemented animals as compared with controls.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The observed diminishment of circulating IGF-1 levels that results from sodium selenite supplementation occurs independently of effects on GH.
source: Together, these data therefore suggest that the observed diminishment of circulating IGF-1 levels that results from sodium selenite supplementation occurs independently of effects on GH.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The mechanism by which sodium selenite supplementation reduces IGF-1 levels in mice represents a difference from the case in rats, wherein selenium supplementation produces an ~80% reduction in the levels of both GH and IGF-1.
source: This represents an obvious difference from the case in rats, wherein selenium supplementation produces an ~80% reduction in the levels of both GH and IGF-1 (Thorlacius-Ussing et al., 1987).
evidence: This is a comparison between the current study's findings and a cited study (Thorlacius-Ussing et al., 1987).

claim: The response to selenomethionine-containing diets was similar to that of sodium selenite-containing diets, albeit somewhat less robust.
source: Overall, we found that the response to the selenomethionine-containing diets was similar to that of sodium selenite-containing diets, albeit somewhat less robust.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Selenomethionine-supplemented male mice showed a dose-dependent protection against diet-induced obesity.
source: For example, selenomethionine-supplemented male mice showed a dose-dependent protection against diet-induced obesity (Figure 6A,D,G,H), with less overall body mass than control-fed littermates (Figure 6A,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, 6D, 6G, and 6H.

claim: Selenomethionine-supplemented male mice had less inguinal and perigonadal adipose tissue than control-fed littermates.
source: As was the case for sodium selenite-supplemented animals, this difference was primarily due to lower adiposity, as we observed less inguinal and perigonadal adipose tissue in selenomethionine-supplemented male mice (Figure 6G,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G and 6H.

claim: Liver mass was not significantly different between selenomethionine-supplemented and control-fed male mice.
source: However, this effect did not extend to liver, as liver mass was not significantly different between experimental and control animals (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The moderate protection against diet-induced obesity observed in selenomethionine-supplemented male mice was not due to calorie restriction.
source: As before, we confirmed that the moderate protection against diet-induced obesity observed was not due to CR, as animals ate the selenomethionine-containing diets comparably to the control diet (Figure 6B), and their food consumption was actually somewhat higher than that of control-fed animals, when normalized for body mass (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: Selenomethionine supplementation can provide a degree of protection against diet-induced obesity.
source: In any case, when taken together with the results for males, our results clearly demonstrate that selenomethionine supplementation can provide a degree of protection against diet-induced obesity
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: MR-like healthspan benefits may be conferred by selenium sources other than sodium selenite.
source: suggesting that MR-like healthspan benefits may be conferred by selenium sources other than sodium selenite.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the selenomethionine data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The LD50 of sodium selenite for mice is ~3.4 mg/kg of body weight when administered by intravenous injection.
source: The median lethal dose (LD50) of sodium selenite for mice is ~3.4 mg/kg of body weight, nearly half that of selenomethionine (~8.8 mg/kg), and the LD50 values for these compounds are similar for rats (Ammar and Couri, 1981; Klug et al., 1952; Shibata et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations (Ammar and Couri, 1981; Klug et al., 1952; Shibata et al., 1992).

claim: The LD50 of selenomethionine for mice is ~8.8 mg/kg of body weight when administered by intravenous injection.
source: The median lethal dose (LD50) of sodium selenite for mice is ~3.4 mg/kg of body weight, nearly half that of selenomethionine (~8.8 mg/kg), and the LD50 values for these compounds are similar for rats (Ammar and Couri, 1981; Klug et al., 1952; Shibata et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations (Ammar and Couri, 1981; Klug et al., 1952; Shibata et al., 1992).

claim: The LD50 of orally ingested sodium selenite is 21.2 mg/kg for mice.
source: A more recent study was performed that found the LD50 of orally ingested sodium selenite to be 21.2 mg/kg for mice (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation (Wang et al., 2017).

claim: At the time of writing, a cohort of animals has been fed the sodium selenite-containing diet continuously for 35 weeks and have remained healthy and without impairment.
source: In fact, at the time of writing, a cohort of animals has been fed the sodium selenite-containing diet continuously for 35 weeks and have remained healthy and without impairment.
evidence: This is a statement about ongoing observations.

claim: Mice fed the sodium selenite-containing diet for 16 weeks featured plasma levels of ALT that were lower than those of control-fed littermates.
source: We found that mice fed the sodium selenite-containing diet for 16 weeks featured plasma levels of ALT, AST, and ALP that were either lower than (ALT) or similar to (AST and ALP) those of control-fed littermates (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Mice fed the sodium selenite-containing diet for 16 weeks featured plasma levels of AST and ALP that were similar to those of control-fed littermates.
source: We found that mice fed the sodium selenite-containing diet for 16 weeks featured plasma levels of ALT, AST, and ALP that were either lower than (ALT) or similar to (AST and ALP) those of control-fed littermates (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and 8C.

claim: It is highly unlikely that mice fed the sodium selenite-containing diet experienced any systemic toxicity.
source: Thus, it is highly unlikely that these animals experienced any systemic toxicity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the liver enzyme data shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: The observed reduction of circulating ALT may represent evidence that selenium supplementation ameliorates liver dysfunction caused by the high-fat diet.
source: Quite the contrary, the observed reduction of circulating ALT may represent evidence that selenium supplementation ameliorates liver dysfunction caused by the high-fat diet.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the ALT data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: No significant difference in free T3 levels was found between mice fed the sodium selenite-containing diet or the control diet for 25 weeks.
source: We therefore measured the levels of free T3 in the plasma of mice fed either the sodium selenite-containing diet or the control diet for 25 weeks. We found no significant difference in T3 levels (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The sodium selenite-containing diet used in the current study is not toxic to mice.
source: Taken together, the above observations indicate that the sodium selenite-containing diet used in the current study is not toxic to mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple toxicity tests shown in Figure 8.

claim: Aging wild-type yeast in selenomethionine-containing medium resulted in a 62% extension of maximum chronological lifespan (21 days vs 13 days) as compared with yeast aged in control medium.
source: We found that aging wild-type yeast in selenomethionine-containing medium resulted in a 62% extension of maximum CLS (21 days vs 13 days; p=0.0164) as compared with yeast aged in control medium (Figure 9A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Selenium supplementation produced a dramatic extension of yeast replicative lifespan, with median survival extended by nine generations (30%) as compared with controls.
source: In addition, selenium supplementation also produced a dramatic extension of RLS, with median survival extended by nine generations (30%; p=0.00008) as compared with controls (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: Supplementing yeast medium with an organoselenium compound produces healthspan benefits detectable by multiple assays of cellular aging.
source: Together, these findings demonstrate that supplementing yeast medium with an organoselenium compound produces healthspan benefits detectable by not just one, but multiple assays of cellular aging.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 9A and 9B.

claim: Mitophagy is required for the extension of yeast chronological lifespan by methionine restriction.
source: Because we previously found the autophagic recycling of mitochondria (i.e., mitophagy) to be indispensable for the extension of CLS by MR (Plummer and Johnson, 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation (Plummer and Johnson, 2019).

claim: Atg32-deficient yeast cells aged in selenomethionine-containing medium failed to demonstrate the extended longevity associated with this intervention.
source: Atg32-deficient cells aged in selenomethionine-containing medium failed to demonstrate the extended longevity associated with this intervention (Figure 9C), instead producing a lifespan curve nearly identical to that of control cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Mitophagy is required for the extension of chronological lifespan by selenium supplementation in yeast.
source: Together, these finding indicate that, similar to the case for MR, mitophagy is required for the extension of CLS by selenium supplementation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Certain organoselenium compounds (including selenomethionine) can be converted by transaminases to their corresponding α-keto acids.
source: In the aforementioned study, the researchers found that certain organoselenium compounds (including selenomethionine) can be converted by transaminases to their corresponding α-keto acids (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation (Lee et al., 2009).

claim: Seleno-α-keto acids are potent histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors.
source: The authors then convincingly demonstrated that these compounds were potent histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors, capable of promoting histone H3 acetylation status.
evidence: Supported by citation (Lee et al., 2009).

claim: Alt1 transaminase activity was required for the full extension of chronological lifespan by selenium supplementation in yeast.
source: The results revealed that transaminase activity was required for the full extension of CLS by selenium supplementation (Figure 9D), as Alt1-deficient cells aged in selenomethionine-containing media demonstrated only a modest extension of CLS as compared with control cells (13 days vs 11 days; p=0.014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Alt1 transaminase activity is not required for the extended chronological lifespan of methionine-restricted yeast cells.
source: Finally, to determine whether Alt1 transaminase activity might be needed specifically for CLS extension by selenium supplementation, or if this activity might instead be required for the extended longevity of yeast in all settings, we tested whether Alt1 deficiency compromised the extended CLS of methionine-restricted cells. We found that the CLS of Alt1-deficient cells was no different from that of wild-type cells (Figure 9E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Alt1 transaminase activity is not required for chronological lifespan extension per se, but specifically for the extension of chronological lifespan by selenium supplementation.
source: indicating that Alt1 transaminase activity is not required for CLS extension, per se, but specifically for the extension of CLS by selenium supplementation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data shown in Figure 9D and 9E.

claim: Binding of IGF-1 to the IGF-1R receptor activates the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, thereby stimulating growth and proliferation, while also impairing autophagy and the response to stress.
source: As for how impairment of IGF-1 signaling promotes healthspan, it is known that binding of IGF-1 to the IGF-1R receptor activates the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, thereby stimulating growth and proliferation, while also impairing autophagy and the response to stress (Bitto et al., 2010; Holzenberger et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations (Bitto et al., 2010; Holzenberger et al., 2003).

claim: Both autophagy and stress response pathways are involved in the regulation of longevity in organisms from yeast to mammals.
source: It has been well established in a variety of organisms, from yeast to mammals, that both autophagy and stress response pathways are involved in the regulation of longevity (Guarente et al., 2008; Postnikoff et al., 2017; Rubinsztein et al., 2011; Tyler and Johnson, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations (Guarente et al., 2008; Postnikoff et al., 2017; Rubinsztein et al., 2011; Tyler and Johnson, 2018).

claim: Integrated stress response factors mediate yeast replicative lifespan.
source: Indeed, we previously found that integrated stress response factors mediate yeast RLS (Hu et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citation (Hu et al., 2018).

claim: Both the retrograde stress response and mitophagy are required for the full extension of yeast chronological lifespan by methionine restriction.
source: and that both the retrograde stress response and the selective autophagic process mitophagy are required for the full extension of yeast CLS by MR (Johnson and Johnson, 2014; Plummer and Johnson, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations (Johnson and Johnson, 2014; Plummer and Johnson, 2019).

claim: The activation of autophagy is sufficient to extend mouse lifespan.
source: In mammals, not only has autophagy been implicated in the benefits of healthspan-extending interventions, but the activation of autophagy is actually sufficient to extend mouse lifespan (Pyo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation (Pyo et al., 2013).

claim: Reduced circulating IGF-1 likely promotes healthspan by de-repressing pro-longevity pathways downstream of PI3K/AKT/mTOR.
source: Thus, reduced circulating IGF-1 likely promotes healthspan by de-repressing pro-longevity pathways downstream of PI3K/AKT/mTOR.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature and experimental data.

claim: Selenium supplementation may reduce circulating IGF-1 in mice independently of effects on growth hormone.
source: As for how selenium supplementation restricts the circulating levels of IGF-1 in mice, our data suggest that this may occur independently of any effects on GH.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Dependent on the presence of the Alt1 transaminase, selenium-supplemented yeast show reduced HDAC activity.
source: For example, like the structurally similar compounds sodium butyrate and β-hydroxybutyrate (βHB), seleno-α-keto acids are potent HDAC inhibitors (Lee et al., 2009) and our studies demonstrate that, dependent on the presence of the Alt1 transaminase, selenium-supplemented yeast show reduced HDAC activity (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1 and citation (Lee et al., 2009).

claim: The administration of β-hydroxybutyrate extends worm lifespan.
source: There might even be a precedent for such a notion, as the administration of βHB extends worm lifespan (Edwards et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation (Edwards et al., 2014).

claim: Both phenylbutyrate and sodium butyrate extend fly lifespan.
source: and both phenylbutyrate and sodium butyrate extend fly lifespan (Kang et al., 2002; Zhao, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations (Kang et al., 2002; Zhao, 2005).

claim: Sodium butyrate is known to ameliorate multiple age-related pathologies in mice and improves survival in a short-lived mouse model.
source: Additionally, sodium butyrate is known to ameliorate multiple age-related pathologies in mice and improves survival in a short-lived mouse model (McIntyre et al., 2019; Ying et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations (McIntyre et al., 2019; Ying et al., 2006).

claim: Butyrate promotes mitochondrial biogenesis.
source: Interestingly, butyrate also promotes mitochondrial biogenesis (Uittenbogaard et al., 2018; Walsh et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations (Uittenbogaard et al., 2018; Walsh et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2019).

claim: Under certain conditions, selenium can interfere with one carbon metabolism.
source: Apparently, under certain conditions, selenium can interfere with one carbon metabolism (Speckmann and Grune, 2015; Speckmann et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations (Speckmann and Grune, 2015; Speckmann et al., 2017).

claim: Nearly all of the MR-associated phenotypes tested in mice are also produced by selenium supplementation.
source: Regarding such differences, as well as the similarities between selenium supplementation and MR, we find that nearly all of the MR-associated phenotypes that we tested in mice are also produced by selenium supplementation.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on all experimental data presented.

claim: Only female mice alter adiponectin levels in response to selenium supplementation, whereas plasma levels of this hormone are increased by MR in both males and females.
source: That said, a notable difference between these interventions is that only female mice alter adiponectin levels in response to selenium supplementation, whereas plasma levels of this hormone are increased by MR in both males and females.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on experimental data shown in Figures 3C and 4C.

claim: MR dramatically increases the levels of FGF-21 in all mice, regardless of their age, whereas FGF-21 does not change in response to selenium supplementation in young (2-month-old) animals.
source: In addition, MR dramatically increases the levels of FGF-21 in all mice, regardless of their age, whereas our results indicate that FGF-21 does not change in response to selenium supplementation in young (2-month-old) animals.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on experimental data shown in Figures 3D and 4D.

claim: An MR-like phenotype is possible in the absence of elevated FGF-21 levels.
source: The latter observation is particularly fascinating, as it demonstrates that an MR-like phenotype is possible in the absence of elevated FGF-21 levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FGF-21 data.

claim: FGF-21 is dispensable for the healthspan benefits associated with methionine restriction.
source: This is consistent with a recent report that FGF-21 is actually dispensable for the healthspan benefits associated with MR (Cooke et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation (Cooke et al., 2020).

claim: Both inorganic selenium sources like sodium selenite and the organoselenium compound selenomethionine have been demonstrated to be safe for human consumption.
source: Importantly, both inorganic selenium sources like sodium selenite and the organoselenium compound selenomethionine have been demonstrated to be safe for human consumption
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the discussion of the SELECT trial.

claim: A large-scale clinical trial (SELECT) has been performed aimed at testing whether selenomethionine supplementation might reduce the incidence of prostate cancer in humans.
source: and, as mentioned above, a large-scale clinical trial (selenium and vitamin E cancer prevention trial; SELECT) has been performed aimed at testing whether selenomethionine supplementation might reduce the incidence of prostate cancer in humans (Klein et al., 2011; Lippman et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations (Klein et al., 2011; Lippman et al., 2009).

claim: The SELECT trial failed to find an anti-tumor effect of selenomethionine supplementation under the conditions tested.
source: While this study failed to find an anti-tumor effect of this intervention under the conditions tested
evidence: Supported by citations (Klein et al., 2011; Lippman et al., 2009).

claim: Selenium availability is positively correlated with human healthspan.
source: Regardless, it has been clear for some time that selenium availability is positively correlated with human healthspan.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by subsequent citations.

claim: Selenium levels fall with age.
source: For example, selenium levels fall with age
evidence: This is a general statement that is part of established knowledge.

claim: Blood selenium levels are highly predictive of human longevity.
source: and studies have demonstrated that blood selenium levels are highly predictive of human longevity (Akbaraly et al., 2005; Olivieri et al., 1994; Ray et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations (Akbaraly et al., 2005; Olivieri et al., 1994; Ray et al., 2006).

claim: Dietary selenium is essential for human health.
source: Not surprisingly, dietary selenium is essential for human health
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: Dietary selenium is required for the function of approximately two dozen selenoproteins, many of which are involved in redox homeostasis and the response to oxidative stress.
source: moreover, it is required for the function of approximately two dozen selenoproteins, many of which are involved in redox homeostasis and the response to oxidative stress (Kryukov et al., 2003; Rayman, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations (Kryukov et al., 2003; Rayman, 2012).

claim: Selenium supplementation has been shown to protect cells against oxidative damage.
source: Indeed, selenium supplementation has been shown to protect cells against oxidative damage (Yoon et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citation (Yoon et al., 2002).

claim: Selenoproteins are known to confer protection against age-associated neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease.
source: and selenoproteins are known to confer protection against age-associated neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation (Zhang et al., 2010).

claim: Selenium supplementation of cultured mouse neurons results in elevated levels of both mitochondrial biogenesis and markers of mitochondrial function.
source: Also, given our findings regarding mitophagy, it is interesting to note that selenium supplementation of cultured mouse neurons was shown to result in elevated levels of both mitochondrial biogenesis and markers of mitochondrial function (Mendelev et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation (Mendelev et al., 2012).

claim: Selenium supplementation downregulates IGF-1 signaling, thereby activating pathways that are both beneficial to healthspan and shared with MR.
source: In the current study, we present a novel mechanism by which selenium supplementation contributes to mammalian healthspan. We propose that this intervention downregulates IGF-1 signaling, thereby activating pathways that are both beneficial to healthspan and shared with MR.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic hypothesis of the study, supported by all experimental data.

claim: In the short term, selenium supplementation results in a total protection against diet-induced obesity.
source: In the short term, this results in a total protection against diet-induced obesity.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: In the long term, selenium supplementation is expected to produce an MR-like extension of overall survival, as well as an amelioration of age-related pathologies.
source: However, we expect that, in the long term, this intervention will also produce an MR-like extension of overall survival, as well as an amelioration of age-related pathologies.
evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the current findings.
